question: Despite common policies and the single market, the conditions for small businesses to access funding differ in Greece and Germany. According to OECD findings published in 2026, Greek micro-enterprises continue to face high collateral requirements and significant loan rejection rates. In 2024, the weighted average interest rate stood at 5.9 % on loans of up to EUR 250 000. Moreover, in 2024 SMEs received only 24.

8 % of all new business loans, according to the OECD. In its 2026 recommendations, the European Commission points out that the Greek venture capital market remains underdeveloped, severely limiting financing for innovative companies during their growth stages. Meanwhile, only 55.95 % of Greek SMEs has achieved a basic level of digital intensity, compared with 71.39 % across the EU as a whole.
The situation raises questions about the effectiveness of Greek government policy and the uneven distribution of European funding between small businesses and large business groups. 1.
How does the Commission assess the differences between Greece and Germany when it comes to borrowing costs, required guarantees and access to finance for small businesses?
Does the Commission intend to strengthen specific financial tools for the innovation, digital upgrading and productive growth of Greek small businesses?

Does it have any data on the distribution of European funds by company size in Greece and is it examining whether the concentration of funding in large groups restricts competition and the opportunities of smaller companies?
